div.p: This paper studies the estimation of a cross-sectional spatial autoregressive (SAR) model with spatial weights constructed by bilateral variables like the trade or investment between regions. We model the possible endogeneity in spatial weights due to the correlation between the error term in the SAR model and unobserved interactive fixed effects in bilateral variables. Using a control function approach, we propose two-stage estimation methods and establish their consistency and asymptotic normality. Finite sample properties are investigated by a Monte Carlo study. We further apply our method to an empirical study of interactions among different US industries through production networks.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In spatial econometrics, the spatial autoregressive (SAR) model has been applied to cases where the outcome of a spatial unit at a location depends not only on its own characteristics but also on outcomes of its neighbors. This model is of great interest to economists because it has a game structure and can be interpreted as a reaction function. Hence, it has been widely used in both economics and social sciences. Typical examples are the technological externality among countries in regional science (Ertur and Koch, 2011), the regional competition among local governments in political science (Bordigon et al., 2003;Allers and Elhorst, 2005), the spillover of housing prices in urban economics (Baltagi et al., 2014), and peer effects among students in labor economics (Lin, 2010), etc. The structure of "neighbors" is fully captured by a spatial weight matrix W n = (w ij ), where w ij is a measure of connections and their strengths among locations i and j as flows in a directed network. 1 Consequently, the spatial dependence parameter measures the magnitude of the interactive/spillover effects based on the neighboring structure W n . Usually, W n is specified before estimating the interactive/spillover effect. Estimation methods for the SAR model have been well studied in the literature: the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) of Ord (1975) and Lee (2004); the instrumental variable (IV) methods of Anselin (1980) and Kelejian andPrucha (1998, 1999), and the generalized method of moments (GMM) of Lee (2007), Liu and Lee (2010), Lin and Lee (2010), and Liu et al. (2010). Consistency and asymptotic normality of these estimators are established using the law of large numbers (LLN) and central limit theorem (CLT) of linear-quadratic statistics. The underlying assumption is that W n is either pre-determined, non-stochastic, or at least exogenous in the sense that elements in w ij would be uncorrelated with unobservables in the outcome equation.

This exogeneity assumption of W n may hold when spatial weights are constructed using pre-determined location information, for example, w ij = 1 if the two locations i and j are adjacent and w ij = 0 otherwise; or w ij is a function of geographic distances and/or exogenous characteristics between different i and j cities, regions, and countries. However, when spatial weights involve endogenous social/economic variables, such as the relative GDP or trade volume, then it is very likely that these elements in w ij are directly correlated with the final outcome. In this case, W n may not be exogenous and estimation methods relying on exogenous W n might not be valid.

In Pinkse and Slade (2010), they point out that endogeneity of spatial weights is challenging and waiting for good solutions, and is one of the future research directions of spatial econometrics. However, due to the technical complication, only few estimation methods have been proposed for estimating spatial models with endogenous weights. Kelejian and Piras (2014) propose using an estimated weight matrix Ŵn to construct valid instruments. To do so, they directly use projections of w ij on exogenous variables to construct instruments. Their idea is straightforward, but it is not easy to find valid instruments, and they can only provide high level assumptions to justify asymptotic properties of their IV estimators. Based on such projections, Cheng and Lee (2017) construct a Hausman test for the endogeneity of the spatial weights matrix. However, the test may have weak powers unless the sample size is sufficiently large. Alternatively, when the spatial weight matrix W n is constructed by some economic variable Z that measures the importance of the relationship between regions, it is desirable to directly model the source of endogeneity and use a control function approach to deal with it. Qu and Lee (2015) consider the case of W n constructed by some vector z of unilateral economic variables w ij = h(z i , z j ), for example, h(z i , z j ) = 1/|z i -z j |. They model the source of endogeneity as the correlation between error terms in the z equation and the SAR equation. This idea is further applied to model endogenous spatial weights in the spatial dynamic panel data model in Qu et al. (2016Qu et al. ( , 2017)).

However, in some empirical cases, relevant economic variables z may be bilateral, namely, w ij = h(z ij , z ji ), where z ij can be a trade volume, a migration flow, or an investment cash flow between regions i and j. For example, when Baicker (2005) uses the SAR model to study the per capita expenditure, one specification of w ij is based on the fraction of all immigrants to state i that comes from state j. Giuliodori and Beetsma (2008) study the primary deficit over GDP using the SAR model and construct the spatial weight w ij by trade-weights as a share of total trade. Ertur and Koch (2011) apply spatial models to study the total factor productivity, and they construct the spatial weight w ij using average imports of country i from country j. Ho et al. (2013) study the spatial spillover in the real GDP per labor, and they construct w ij using the sum of export and import flows between i and j. According to the gravity model which is widely used for international trade, imports and exports between two regions can be affected by unobservable multilateral resistance of each region, which might be correlated with the unobservables in the outcome equation. Similarly, for other cases like immigration, the unobservables generating the bilateral variables could be correlated with those generating outcomes. Unfortunately, many researchers still treat W n as exogenous and apply conventional methods for estimation and inference. In general, when endogeneity in W n was ignored, estimators would be biased and inconsistent. Then, how to model this endogeneity in W n coming from bilateral economic variables? How to consistently estimate and give inference to parameters of interest? These are the motivated issues for study in this paper.

As the economic variable z is bilateral, modeling and estimation methods in Qu and Lee (2015) cannot be directly applied. We need to extend it to allow for bilateral economic variables, propose new estimation methods, and establish corresponding asymptotic properties. To explicitly model the source of potential endogeneity of W n from bilateral economic variables, we build two sets of equations -one is for the SAR outcome y, and the other is a factor model for the bilateral variable z which enters the spatial weights matrix W n . The source of endogeneity is captured by the correlation between error terms in the SAR outcome y equation and unobserved interactive fixed effects in the z equation. As an extension, besides bilateral economic variables, one may also incorporate endogenous univariate variables in W n . We suggest overcoming this endogeneity problem by using a control function approach and propose two-stage estimation methods. As bilateral endogenous variables are our main interest, we first focus on the estimation with only bilateral endogenous variables. In the first stage, unobserved factors and their loadings in the bilateral variable z equation are estimated. In the second stage, we add those two estimates into the SAR model as two additional sets of regressors and then apply the conventional IV or MLE approach to this augmented SAR equation. We show the proposed two-stage estimators are consistent and have asymptotic normality. Based on those, we can directly test the endogeneity through the significance of estimated parameters of the additional sets of regressors. The estimation methods are then extended to the case with both endogenous univariate and bilateral variables.

Notice that we focus on spatial spillover effects of spatial units, which are different from those in the literature of social networks. In a recent working paper of Johnsson and Moon (2019), they consider the estimation of peer effects in endogenous social networks. Our paper is different from theirs in several aspects. First of all, their w ij is either zero or one because it measures whether two individuals are linked, while our w ij is a flexible function (can be continuous or an indicator function) of economic variables. Secondly and most importantly, they model their binary weight using a symmetric function of unobserved dyad attributes, while we model the bilateral variable using a factor model and explicitly address the asymmetric feature in these unobservables. Our model specification is motivated by the trade literature from the direction of the inflow/outflow data that provide enough information to estimate the source and destination regions' effects. Also, in their identification, they require the monotonicity in unobserved effects, but our identification does not impose such a requirement. The two papers propose different implementations of the control function. Our setting is a SAR model where spatial weights are constructed by economic variables measuring the "economic distance" or "economic similarity". Therefore, geographic locations and spatial structures play an important role to guarantee sparsity and weak dependence of spatial units. In a social network, there is no clear measure of the location of an individual, and network links are 0 or 1, which does not guarantee sparsity specifically. When considering the estimation of those models, due to different endogenous weights, the asymptotic analysis will be different.

There are two main contributions of our paper. The first contribution comes from a natural but non-trivial extension of modeling a spatial weights matrix in Qu and Lee (2015). We extend the SAR model with unilateral endogenous variables to allow both endogenous unilateral and bilateral variables in w ij , so we believe that our study may benefit empirical researchers to consistently estimate spatial spillover effects when they construct spatial weight matrix using richer economic variables. As the asymptotic analysis is quite different from that in Qu and Lee (2015), our paper might also be beneficial to theoretical estimation approaches with endogenous spatial/network relations. Secondly, we model our bilateral economic variables using a factor model of interactive fixed effects, which nests the two-way fixed effects model used in the international trade literature as a special example. Then, the source of endogeneity has a clear economic meaning as the correlation between those unobservables and error terms in the outcome equation, which helps us to understand the channel of endogeneity, and hence better analyzing and interpreting the spatial spillover effect.

The rest of the paper is as follows: Section 2 sets up the model. Section 3 introduces 2-stage estimation approaches. Their consistency and asymptotic distributions are established in Section 4. Finite sample properties of our proposed estimators are investigated in Section 5 by a Monte Carlo (MC) study. Section 6 applies our estimation methods to empirically study interactions among different industries through the input/output networks. Section 7 extends the model to allow both unilateral and bilateral economics variables to construct w ij . Section 8 concludes the paper. The MLE derivations and the construction of the Input-Output relations are in Appendix A. Detailed proofs and additional MC results are provided in the supplementary file. 2

div.head: Model
div.p: The outcome y at the location i is modeled with a cross-sectional SAR equation of

div.p: where i = 1, . . . , n is the spatial unit, x i is a k-dimensional vector of observed exogenous characteristics at location i including the constant, v i is the error term, the spatial weight w ij measures the connections and their strengths among
div.formula: locations i ̸ = j (w ii = 0 for all i), so ∑ j̸ =i w ij y j is the outcome of i's neighbors, the scalar λ is the spatial coefficient, β is a k-dimensional parameter. Define the n-dimensional vectors Y n = (y 1 , . . . , y n ) ′ and V n = (v 1 , . . . , v n ) ′
div.p: , and the n × k matrix X n = (x 1 , . . . , x n ) ′ . Then, we can write the SAR model in the matrix form as 3
div.formula: Y n = λW n Y n + X n β + V n . (2.2)
div.p: In this paper, we consider a spatial weight constructed by some bilateral variable z ij , i.e., w ij = h(z ij , z ji ), where h(•) is a known function. Typical examples can be the trade volume, the migration flow, and the foreign direct investment between the two countries i and j. We model this bilateral variable z ij by the regression equation
div.formula: z ij = c z + ϕ ij α + η ′ 1i η 2j + ε ij , (2.3)
div.p: where c z is a constant, ϕ ij is a vector of exogenous variables and α is its associated slope parameter vector, η 1i and η 2j are r-dimensional unobserved interactive fixed effects (FE) motivated by the panel factor model, 4 which includes conventional additive fixed effects as a special case, and ε ij is the idiosyncratic error.
2 The supplementary file is online of this journal.

3 We use lowercase letters for vectors representing individual characteristics, fixed effects, and outcomes, and uppercase letters for characters and outcomes of the whole sample. The subscript n for a lowercase letter in some occasions shows the identity of the nth individual (in general, we use a subscript i to represent an arbitrary individual) and the subscript n for an uppercase letter represents the sample size. So we have decided to take the simpler option on indexing all variables without an additional subscript n. This is so because in our spatial weight matrix, there are flow variables which have already double subscripts. If we adopt another index n, we would have triple indices for flow variables, which would seem too much. 4 We note that these effects would be different from the model where η 1i = η 2i for all i, which can be regarded as an error component model.

Here the effects η 1i and η 2i are not restricted to be the same. For example, if i is an exporter and j is an importer, their individual effects would be different due to their different roles in the trade. This specification is relevant to panel data models with individual effects interacted with time effects. In our model, the "time period" and the number of individual units are the same, while in a panel model, they are usually not the same.
Here, to fix the idea and simplify the notation, we use a standard SAR model for y. The same analysis also applies to the spatial Durbin model, i.e.,
div.formula: y i = λ ∑ j̸ =i w ij y j + x ′ i β + ∑ j̸ =i w ij x j δ + v i , so not only i's neighbors outcome ∑ j̸ =i w ij y j but also i's neighbors characteristics ∑ j̸ =i w ij x j might directly affect y i . 5

div.head: A motivating example: The gravity model
div.p: The generation of the bilateral variable is motivated by the gravity example. The outcome TFP (total factor productivity) y has the technological spillover that
div.formula: y i = λ ∑ j̸ =i w ij y j + x ′ i β + v i , (2.4)
div.p: where in the spatial weight w ij = h(z ij , z ji ), z ij is the log value of export from i to j, and z ji is the log value of j's export to i. For example, w ij is constructed purely by the import from j by i in Ertur and Koch (2011), i.e., w ij = exp(z ji ); w ij is constructed by the summation of i's export to and import from j in de Mooij et al. (2005) and Ho et al. (2013), i.e., w ij = exp(z ij + z ji ).
From the gravity model, the international trade literature derives the following equation for the export:
div.formula: Ept ij = ( G i G j G w ) ( T ij Pi Pj ) 1-σ ,
div.p: where Ept ij is the total export of country i to country j, G i and G j are the GDP of country i and j, G
div.formula: w = ∑ n i=1 G i is the
div.p: world GDP, T ij is the transport cost related to the geographic distance of i and j, and the cross-border effect, Pi and Pj are called "indices of multilateral resistance" in Anderson and van Wincoop (2003). These indices are unobserved, so the trade literature has several different ways to proxy or estimate them. For the detailed model derivation, structure interpretation, and results comparison, see the survey in Feenstra (2003). Subsequently, the following econometrics model is recommended:
div.formula: ln(Ept ij /G i G j ) = α 1 ln d ij + γ 1 (1 -b ij ) + δ i 1 + δ j 2 + ε ij ,
div.p: where d ij is the geographic distance between country i and j, b ij is a dummy variable related to the cross-border or some trade treaty, δ i 1 is the exporter fixed effects, δ j 2 is the importer fixed effects. In this setting, the coefficients δ i 1 and δ j 2 provide estimates of the multilateral resistance terms (average trade barriers faced by an importer and an exporter), and ε ij is the idiosyncratic shock. Feenstra (2003) comments "the fixed effects method produces consistent estimates of the average border effect across countries, and is simple to implement, so it might be considered to be the preferred empirical method". This example is a special case of our proposed model
div.formula: z ij = c z + ϕ ij α + η ′ 1i η 2j + ε ij , (2.5) with c z = γ 1 , ϕ ij = (ln d ij , b ij ), η 1i = (1, δ i 1 ) ′
div.p: , and η 2j = (δ j 2 , 1) ′ . With interactive fixed effects allowed, our model is capable of characterizing the asymmetry of the marginal effects of unobservable individual heterogeneity. In the gravity model, with multilateral resistance treated as one-dimensional additive fixed effects, if δ i 1 < δ k 1 , compared to k, country i would have more exports to any other third country j, with other characteristics controlled equally. With a multi-dimensional factor structure, however, we can use η 1i to represent i's trade advantage in different industries and η 2j as j's protection policies in corresponding sectors. Therefore, it is possible that i enjoys a comparative advantage in agricultural production and exports more to j in agriculture than k; and k is better at manufacture and exports more manufactured goods to j than i. With a more flexible framework on endogenous bilateral variables, our model can be applied to analyze more issues, such as inter-sectoral spillovers through input-output networks, which is analyzed in the empirical part.

div.head: Estimation
div.p: Our estimation for the SAR outcome equation is based on the control function approach such that
div.formula: y i = λ ∑ j̸ =i w ij y j + x ′ i β + c + η i ρ + ξ i ,(3.1)
div.p: where c = -µ ′ η ρ is a constant, which shall be absorbed by the intercept term if there is a constant intercept in x i . So for this intercept issue, we may assume that x i does not include a constant term and c is a free intercept coefficient. Once we control for the unobserved effect η i , the remaining error term ξ i is uncorrelated with regressors x i and the weight w ij for all j ̸ = i. Since η i is unobservable but can be consistently estimated, we propose two-stage estimation methods for the SAR equation in (3.1).

div.p: In the 1st stage, we estimate equation (2.3) and get estimates for all the interactive fixed effects η1i and η2i by the principal components estimators in Bai (2003). We need to normalize some parameters to identify these interactive fixed effects, otherwise there exist multiple sets of parameter values that satisfy the model specification. Following Bai (2009a), we normalize η ′ 1n η 1n /n = I r and η ′ 2n η 2n to be diagonal.

div.head: The second stage estimators
div.p: To establish the asymptotic properties of our estimator, we list some regularity conditions. Following Jenish andPrucha (2009, 2012), we consider spatial processes located on a (possibly) unevenly spaced lattice D ⊆ R d 0 , d 0 ≥ 1. Asymptotic methods we employ are increasing domain asymptotics: growth of the sample is ensured by an unbounded expansion of the sample region as in Jenish and Prucha (2012). 10 Assumption 2. The lattice D ⊂ R d 0 , d 0 ≥ 1, is infinitely countable. The location l : {1, . . . , n} → D n ⊂ D is a mapping of individual i to its location l(i) ∈ D n ⊂ R d 0 . All elements in D are located at distances of at least s 0 > 0 from each other, i.e., ∀l(i), l(j) ∈ D : d ij ≥ s 0 , where d ij is the distance between individuals i and j (locations l(i) and l(j)); w.l.o.g. we assume that s 0 = 1.

As our asymptotic analysis is based on inference in increasing domain but not for infill asymptotics, physical distance plays an important role in keeping agents apart from each other. For the case of pure economic distance, if there were economic factors which keep agents apart, we might replace the "physical distance'' in Assumption 2 by economic distance.
Assumption 3. For any i, j, and n, the spatial weight w ij ≥ 0, w ii = 0, and sup n ∥W n ∥ ∞ = c w < ∞. The spatial coefficient λ satisfies sup λ∈Λ |λ|c w < 1, where Λ is the parameter space for λ.
Assumption 3 is standard in the spatial econometrics literature to limit the spatial correlation in a manageable degree.

Assumption 4. We consider the spatial weight matrix W n that can be either row-normalized or normalized using the spectral norm. Before normalization, w * ij = h ij (z ij , z ji , d ij ) for i ̸ = j, where h ij (•)'s are non-negative, uniformly bounded functions of some observable variable Z such that 0 ≤ w * ij ≤ c 1 d ij -c 0 d 0 for some 0 ≤ c 1 and c 0 > 3 + 1/d 0 . 11 Furthermore, there exist at most K (K ≥ 1) columns of W n that the column sum exceeds c w , where K is a fixed number that does not depend n. 12 To ensure the valid row-normalization, we assume there are no isolated locations, i.e., there exists a finite distance r 0 such that for any i,
div.formula: ∑ j∈B i (r 0 ) w * ij ≥ c > 0, where B i (r)

div.head: Test the endogeneity
div.p: Since the endogeneity of W n comes from the unobserved fixed effects η n , to test the endogeneity in W n , we can simply test the irrelevance of η n , i.e., test the significance of the associated coefficient ρ with H 0 : ρ = 0 and H 1 : ρ ̸ = 0. As ρ is directly estimated in our 2nd Stage, we can construct the Wald test statistic nρ ′ V (ρ) -1 ρ d → χ 2 r * , where V (ρ) is the estimated variance-covariance matrix for √ nρ. We reject H 0 at the significance level α s if nρ ′ V (ρ) -1 ρ exceeds the (1-α s ) percentile of the χ 2 distribution with the degree of freedom r * . For example, if r * = 2 (interactive fixed effects with r = 1 or additive two-way fixed effects), we reject the null of no endogeneity in W n at the 10%, 5%, and 1% significance levels if nρ ′ V (ρ) -1 ρ exceeds respectively 4.605, 5.991, and 9.210.

div.head: Empirical application
div.p: In this section, we apply the model to investigate interactions among different "industries", or "sectors". The idea that different industries (or "sectors") are connected through input-output linkages and idiosyncratic shocks can translate and propagate through a network dates back to Long and Plosser (1983) and is developed by Acemoglu et al. (2012). In their general-equilibrium models about a multi-sectoral economy, outputs produced by one sector can be used both as the final goods consumed by consumers and production intermediary inputs employed by other sectors. As a result, shocks to the production of one sector may influence the production of sectors who use its outputs and also those who make its inputs. After scrutinizing the input-output network structure, Acemoglu et al. (2012) relate the aggregate volatility of the economy to network features characterized by two measures: the network degrees and the Bonacich centrality vector. 15In this way, they explain why shocks in one sector cannot always be disaggregated even when the number of sectors increases. Input-output linkages were viewed as exogenous in Long and Plosser (1983), Acemoglu et al. (2012) and other early research papers. More recently, researchers model them as determined by choices of consumers and firms, such as Acemoglu and Azar (2020) and Dong and Wen (2019). In those structural models, tractable closed-form solutions usually rely on assumptions on specific forms for utility and production functions. In this section, we show how to quantitatively characterize this type of interactions using publicly available census or survey data, with the endogeneity brought about by industry-specific unobservables.

We employed the 6-digit detail-level input-output information from BEA. This data set is renewed every five years, and the most recent two sets of tables are for the Year 2007 and 2012. From the NBER-CES database, we can get information on value-added, labor, and capital used for detail-level manufacture industries only till 2011. 16 As both data are available only for 2007, we use that cross-sectional data to analyze cross-industry interactions on value added: 9617 Note: ''Input Direct requirements'' measures the dollar values of inputs required directly from other sectors to produce a unit of output of a downstream industry. ''Output Supplies'' correspond to the shares of outputs sold to other industries as production intermediaries normalized by the suppliers' total sales. Summing up the total inputs of a downstream industry and the total outputs supplied by an upstream industry, we get ''total input direct requirements'' and ''total output supplies''. div.head: Conclusion
div.p: This paper studies the specification and 2-stage estimation methods (2SIV and 2SML) of a cross-sectional SAR/SDM model with spatial weights constructed by endogenous bilateral variables. We build two sets of equations: one for the SAR outcome, and the other for the bilateral economic variable that constructs spatial weights. We argue that the unobserved interactive effects in the bilateral variable and the error term in the SAR outcome equation can be correlated and hence cause the endogeneity in spatial weights. We establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the 2SIV and the 2SML estimators, investigate their finite sample properties by a Monte Carlo study. We use our model and estimation methods to study the productivity of industries in the U.S. The empirical results are more revealing and interesting once the interactive fixed effects are controlled for.

div.head: Construction of the input-output relations
div.p: The bilateral variable, z d i,j , which measures the dollar values of output produced by j demanded by i to produce a dollar value of i's output corresponds to the ''direct requirements'' to industry j by industry i. In a multi-sector economy, an industry is composed of firms and institutes producing analogous products or services, which is called "commodities". A commodity may be produced by different industries. An industry can also produce more than one type of commodities. Hence, in calculating the input-output requirements, we take into account the multiplicity of both inputs and outputs and use both the "use" and "make" tables. The rows and columns of the "use" table, U = (U c,k ), correspond, respectively, to commodities and industries. The elements of the cth row show the use of Commodity c by industries, while the elements of the kth columns present the dollar value of each commodity component used by industry k. With U, we can construct the commodity-by-industry direct requirements matrix B = (B ck ), where
div.formula: B ck = U ck ∑ c ′ U c ′ k
div.p: , with each B ck representing the shares of commodity c used per dollar value of k's production. The rows and columns of the "make" table, V = (V lc ), however, represent industries and commodities. The lth row shows the value of each type of commodity produced by industry l; and the cth column shows the dollar value of the production of commodity c by each industry. From V , we can derive the industry-by-commodity market shares, S = (S lc ), with
div.formula: S lc = V lc ∑ h V hc
div.p: . These market shares need to be adjusted for scrap, a byproduct of production. For each industry (row of the "make" table), we can compute the ratio of non-scrap production. By dividing S lc by the corresponding non-scrap production ratio for row l, we can get the adjusted market share production matrix, M. Then the industry-by-industry direct requirements table/matrix is MB, 24 where the (l, k) element of the matrix D = MB, D lk = ∑ c M lc B ck , measures the value of supplier l's production used as inputs to produce 1 unit of customer k's output. We can see z d ij = D ji . In addition, k might use products of other industries, say industry l ′ , as inputs, and l ′ may also input l's output as inputs. In this way, k uses l's products in an indirect way. Therefore, there is another measure for the input-output relationships, the total requirements, measured by elements of the matrix (I -MB) -1 . 25 As the total requirement combines the use of intermediaries across all the sectors, to focus on the bilateral relationship between two industries, we focus on the measure of direct requirements in this paper. The bilateral variables we used satisfy z d ij = D ji , for i ̸ = j. For definitions and calculations of the "use" and "make" tables, direct and total requirements, please refer to the I/O table manual provided by BEA. In constructing the matrix for direct requirements, we take care of the concordance between the 2012 NAICS codes that BEA tables used and the 1997 NAICS codes that the NBER CES Manufacturing Industry Database used.
